title: How to automate markdowns for slow-moving multichannel inventory
body_markdown:
Slow-moving SKUs sitting across Amazon, Walmart, eBay, Shopify, and Etsy don't fix themselves — they eat storage fees while manual repricing lags weeks behind reality. This guide walks through building a markdown automation system that triggers price cuts by sell-through rate instead of gut feel, synced across every channel from one dashboard.


**TL;DR**

- Automate markdowns slow moving inventory by triggering price cuts off sell-through rate, not calendar guesses.
- A three-tier cadence (15% at day 30, 30% at day 60, 50% at day 90) clears dead stock before 2026 storage fees compound.
- SellerChamp syncs markdown rules across Amazon, Walmart, eBay, Shopify, and Etsy from one dashboard — no per-channel manual repricing.
- Multichannel sellers who skip automated markdowns typically hold inventory 2-3x longer than sellers who tier discounts by velocity.


## Why this matters

Every week a slow SKU sits at full price, it's tying up cash and warehouse space you could put into inventory that actually turns. Amazon's long-term storage fees kick in hard after 2026 inventory sits past the 365-day mark, and Walmart and eBay both penalize sellers whose listings show stale sell-through in their internal ranking signals.

Manual markdowns don't scale once you're running listings across five or six marketplaces. You either discount too late (after the fees already hit) or too early (leaving margin on the table). Automated markdown rules solve both problems by tying the discount trigger to actual velocity data instead of a person remembering to check a spreadsheet.

## What you'll need

- **A centralized inventory and listing dashboard.** [SellerChamp](https://sellerchamp.com/) pulls order and stock data from Amazon, eBay, Walmart, Shopify, and Etsy into one view so markdown rules apply everywhere at once instead of channel-by-channel.
- **90 days of sell-through history per SKU.** You can't set velocity thresholds without knowing what "slow" actually means for that product.
- **A markdown tier structure.** Decide your discount steps before you automate anything — most sellers land on three tiers.
- **Repricing rules or a repricer tool.** Something has to execute the price change the moment a SKU crosses a threshold.
- **A cutoff point.** Every automated markdown plan needs a floor — the price where you stop discounting and liquidate or bundle instead.

## The steps

### 1. Pull sell-through rate by SKU across every channel

Sell-through rate — units sold divided by units available, over a set window — is the number that should trigger every markdown, not days-on-shelf alone. A SKU that sells slowly on Etsy but moves fine on Shopify needs a channel-specific view, not a blended average that hides the problem.

Calculate this weekly, not monthly. A 30-day lag between a stall and your first price cut is 30 days of storage fees and tied-up cash you don't get back. Common mistake: pulling sell-through only from your primary channel and assuming it reflects Amazon or Walmart performance — it almost never does.

### 2. Set velocity thresholds that define "slow-moving"

Pick a number and commit to it: for most multichannel sellers, anything under 15% sell-through in a 30-day window qualifies as slow. Fast fashion and seasonal goods need tighter windows (14-21 days); durable goods can run 45-60 days before a stall counts as a real problem.

Write the threshold into your rules engine, not into a person's memory. The point of automation is removing the judgment call at the moment of truth.

### 3. Build a three-tier markdown cadence

A simple, defensible structure: 15% off at day 30 of slow status, 30% off at day 60, 50% off at day 90. Each tier fires automatically once the SKU crosses the prior day threshold without improving sell-through.

This cadence gives the market three chances to absorb the product before you're forced into a full liquidation markdown. Skipping straight to 50% at day 30 trains repeat buyers to wait you out — a mistake sellers with loyal storefronts feel fast.

### 4. Sync the markdown rule across every marketplace simultaneously

This is where manual processes break down. A price change made in Seller Central doesn't touch your Shopify storefront or your eBay listing unless something connects them. Run the markdown through a centralized platform so the same SKU updates on Amazon, Walmart, eBay, Shopify, and Etsy in one push instead of five separate logins.

Inconsistent pricing across channels is one of the fastest ways to trigger a buy box loss on Amazon or a policy flag on Walmart — both platforms compare your price against your own listings elsewhere before they compare you to competitors.


**Automate markdowns across every channel**

Sync inventory, pricing, and listings for Amazon, Walmart, eBay, Shopify, and Etsy in one dashboard.

**[See how it works](https://sellerchamp.com/)**


### 5. Set a hard floor and an exit plan

Decide upfront what happens if a SKU hits your day-90 markdown and still hasn't moved. Options: bundle it with a faster-moving SKU, route it to a liquidation channel, or pull it from marketplaces where storage fees are compounding fastest.

Without a floor, markdown automation just delays the inevitable instead of solving it — you end up giving product away at 70% off with no plan for what's left.

### 6. Monitor margin impact weekly, not after the quarter closes

Track gross margin by SKU alongside the markdown tier it's sitting in. A SKU that needed a 50% cut to move probably has a sourcing or pricing problem upstream, not just a marketing problem.

Expected outcome: within one 90-day cycle, sell-through on tagged slow-movers should climb 20-40 percentage points versus the pre-automation baseline, freeing up storage capacity for inventory that actually turns.

### 7. Rebuild the threshold quarterly

What counted as slow in Q1 2026 might be normal in Q4 if category demand shifts. Revisit your velocity threshold and markdown percentages every quarter rather than treating the rule as permanent.

Common mistake: leaving a 2025 markdown cadence in place through a full seasonal cycle and wondering why fast-moving holiday SKUs get discounted right alongside genuinely dead stock.

## Troubleshooting

- **Markdowns triggering on SKUs that just launched.** New listings have no sell-through baseline — exclude anything under 30 days old from automated markdown rules until it has real velocity data.
- **Price drops on one channel but not others.** This usually means the sync between your inventory system and one marketplace's API is lagging or broken — check the channel connection before assuming the rule failed.
- **Buy box loss right after a markdown.** Amazon sometimes needs 24-48 hours to reflect a new price in buy box eligibility; don't panic-adjust again during that window.
- **Margin dropping faster than sell-through is improving.** Your tiers are probably too aggressive for the category — pull back the day-30 discount to 10% and re-test.
- **Customers price-matching across your own channels.** If Etsy and Shopify show different prices on the same product, tighten your sync frequency — daily at minimum during an active markdown cycle.
- **Storage fees still climbing despite markdowns.** The discount isn't the problem — the floor and exit plan are missing. Set a hard day-120 liquidation trigger.

## Tools and resources

- A multichannel inventory platform that pushes price and stock updates to Amazon, eBay, Walmart, Shopify, and Etsy simultaneously — this is the backbone of any markdown automation setup.
- A repricing engine that can read sell-through velocity, not just competitor price.
- A weekly reporting cadence, even a simple spreadsheet pulling sell-through by SKU, until your rules engine is fully trusted.
- Marketplace-specific fee calculators (Amazon's storage fee schedule, Walmart's WFS fee tool) to model when a markdown pays for itself versus when liquidation is cheaper.

## FAQ


**What is the best way to automate markdowns for slow-moving inventory?**

The best way to automate markdowns for slow moving inventory is tying price cuts to sell-through rate thresholds, not fixed calendar dates. A three-tier cadence — 15% at day 30, 30% at day 60, 50% at day 90 — synced across every marketplace gives the clearest results in 2026.

**How do I know when a SKU counts as slow-moving?**

Most multichannel sellers set the threshold at under 15% sell-through in a rolling 30-day window. Seasonal or fast-fashion categories should use a tighter 14-21 day window since demand shifts faster.

**Is automated markdown pricing better than manual repricing?**

Yes, automated markdown pricing outperforms manual repricing on multichannel accounts because it removes the lag between a stall and the price change. Manual processes across five or six marketplaces routinely run 2-4 weeks behind actual sell-through data.

**How much should I discount slow-moving inventory?**

Start at 15% for the first 30 days of slow status, then step up to 30% and 50% if sell-through doesn't recover. Going straight to a deep discount trains repeat buyers to wait for the next markdown instead of buying at full price.

**Can markdown rules sync across Amazon, Walmart, and Shopify at once?**

Yes, a centralized multichannel platform can push the same price rule to Amazon, Walmart, eBay, Shopify, and Etsy simultaneously. Inconsistent pricing across your own channels is a common trigger for buy box loss on Amazon.

**What happens if a markdown still doesn't move the product?**

Set a hard floor, usually around day 90-120, where the SKU gets bundled, liquidated, or pulled from high-storage-fee channels. Markdown automation without an exit plan just delays the loss instead of solving it.

**Do markdowns hurt profit margin?**

Markdowns reduce margin on that SKU, but the alternative — paying storage fees on dead stock indefinitely — usually costs more over a 90-day cycle. Track margin by SKU weekly to catch cadences that are cutting too deep too fast.

**How often should markdown thresholds be reviewed?**

Review velocity thresholds and discount percentages every quarter, since what counts as slow in one season can be normal demand in another. A cadence built for Q1 2026 holiday leftovers won't fit a Q3 2026 launch cycle.


## One last thing

The sellers who get the most out of markdown automation aren't the ones with the deepest discounts — they're the ones who set the day-30 threshold tight enough to act before storage fees compound, then leave the rule alone instead of second-guessing it every week. Build the cadence once, sync it across every channel, and let the sell-through data make the call in 2026.
